what: Tulsīdās's Rāmcaritmānas draws on the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa: the Śiva-Pārvatī frame, Rāma as Brahman with Sītā as his power, the nine means of devotion to Śabarī, Lakṣmaṇa's consolation of Guha.

evidence.detail: AR 3.10.22-27 and RCM Araṇyakāṇḍa (Śabarī); AR Ayodhyā and RCM Ayodhyā 92-93 (Lakṣmaṇa and Guha)
widely accepted

what: Mutual association of Advaita and Śrīvidyā: Śrīcakra worship in the Śaṅkara maṭhas (tradition), Śākta works ascribed to Gauḍapāda and Śaṅkara (Saundaryalaharī), the Tripura Rahasya's Advaita.

evidence.detail: The maṭhas' worship of Śāradā/Kāmākṣī with the Śrīcakra; attributions of Subhagodaya to Gauḍapāda and Saundaryalaharī to Śaṅkara (disputed).
Scholars doubt the attributions and date the association later.

what: Rasa theory applied to devotion: bhakti as a rasa (Madhusūdana's Bhaktirasāyana).

evidence.detail: Bhaktirasāyana treats devotion in the vocabulary of rasa.

what: The rasa framework (sthāyibhāva, vibhāva, anubhāva, sāttvika, vyabhicārin; the list of transient emotions) of Bharata's school, recast as bhakti-rasa with five primary and seven secondary rasas.

evidence.detail: BRS southern division uses the Nāṭyaśāstra's categories
Rūpa's Nāṭakacandrikā follows Bharata's dramaturgy

what: The Tamil hymns of the Āḻvārs as a second, Tamil Veda; the theology of surrender, of Śrī's mediation and of the Lord's accessibility in temple images; temple recitation.

evidence.detail: Nāthamuni received the Prabandham from Nammāḻvār
Yāmuna salutes Nammāḻvār as the first head of the clan; the Tiruvāymoḻi commentaries

what: The fifteen limbs read as knowledge, and the list of obstacles in samādhi, shared between the Aparokṣānubhūti and the Tejobindu.

evidence.detail: Tejobindu 1.15–41 closely parallels the Aparokṣānubhūti's fifteen limbs

what: The Atharvaveda's highest Brahman, the self 'knowing whom one does not fear death', the city of Brahman in the body, the Full, and Prāṇa as lord of all

evidence.detail: AVŚ 10.8.44 (the fearless self), 10.2.28–33 (the city of Brahman), 10.8.29 (from the full the full), 11.4 (Prāṇa) have close Upaniṣadic parallels (e.g. BĀU 5.1.1; Praśna 2).

what: The ash vow called pāśupata and a verbal parallel: 'having cut the root of the net of causes ... with the intellect ... fixed on Rudra'.

evidence.detail: Atharvaśiras 5 '... hitvā hetujālasya mūlam | buddhyā sañcitaṃ sthāpayitvā tu rudre' ~ PS 5.35-38 'chittvā doṣāṇāṃ hetujālasya mūlam | buddhyā | sañcittam | sthāpayitvā ca rudre'.

notes: Which text borrowed from which is not settled.

what: Atharvavedic healing (bhaiṣajya) and the status of Āyurveda as a limb (upāṅga/upaveda) of the Atharvaveda

evidence.detail: Suśruta Saṃhitā Sūtrasthāna 1.6 calls Āyurveda an upāṅga of the Atharvaveda; Caraka Saṃhitā Sūtrasthāna 30.21 enjoins devotion to the Atharvaveda (loci from memory, moderate).

what: Śaiva ascetic heritage: the five brahma-mantras, ash-observances, the Śaiva cosmos of principles

evidence.detail: historians (A. Sanderson and others) derive the Mantramārga from an Atimārga background; the texts themselves rank the Atimārga below the Mantramārga

what: The proof of the self's existence given in Śabara's pramāṇa section, which Śaṅkara says was drawn from the Śārīraka (BS 3.3.53); Upavarṣa deferred the topic to the Śārīraka.

evidence.detail: Śaṅkara, BSBh 3.3.53

what: Vocabulary of debate — proposition, reason, example, application, conclusion, quibble, point of defeat — shared by Caraka's debate manual and the Nyāya Sūtra

evidence.detail: Caraka Saṃhitā, Vimānasthāna 8 lists the 'paths of debate' (recalled; to be checked).

what: The Bhagavad Gītā's form — a god teaching a hero/king, vibhūti and viśvarūpa chapters, field-and-knower and three-guṇa chapters — is taken over by the Īśvara, Devī, Śiva and Gaṇeśa Gītās (the Gaṇeśa Gītā reworks many verses with Gaṇeśa as the Lord).
era: first and early second millennium CE (scholarly)

evidence.detail: viśvarūpa: Devī Gītā 7.33, Śiva Gītā 7, Gaṇeśa Gītā 8; Śiva's dance vision in Īśvara Gītā 2.5
the later Gītās are widely read as sectarian responses to the Bhagavad Gītā

what: The ninefold devotion (śravaṇa, kīrtana, smaraṇa…), re-addressed to Śambhu
era: by the time of the SSM

evidence.detail: SSM 9.2–3 parallels Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.5.23 ('śravaṇaṃ kīrtanaṃ viṣṇoḥ…') with Śambhu in place of Viṣṇu.

what: the fourfold form (vyūha) doctrine and Sātvata worship of Vāsudeva
era: scholarly: c. 1st c. BCE – 5th c. CE

evidence.detail: the Nārāyaṇīya calls its teaching 'Pañcarātra' (12.326.100) and names the fourfold form (12.326.68–69)
the Pāñcarātra Saṃhitās trace their teaching to Nārāyaṇa's revelation

what: the Lord's manifestations and Kṛṣṇa devotion

evidence.detail: the Nārāyaṇīya's list of manifestations (12.326.72–94) and BhG 4.7–8 prefigure the Purāṇic avatāra lists; the Harivaṃśa's life of Kṛṣṇa is continued in the Viṣṇu and Bhāgavata Purāṇas

what: The list of the sage's qualities of Bhāgavata 11.11.29-31 is reproduced nearly verbatim in Avadhūta Gītā 8.2-4.

evidence.detail: verified in the local texts
direction assumed from the Bhāgavata to the Avadhūta Gītā (U06 judgement, moderate)

what: The Bhāgavata Purāṇa as the supreme scripture ('the spotless Purāṇa'), source of Kṛṣṇa's status as svayaṃ bhagavān and of the rāsa and gopī theology.

evidence.detail: Tattvasandarbha; Kṛṣṇasandarbha

what: The Bhāgavata as the fourth authority and the ground of puṣṭi (poṣaṇa = anugraha) and nirodha.

evidence.detail: Tattvārthadīpanibandha 1.7; Subodhinī

what: The six means of knowledge (including postulation and non-apprehension) and intrinsic validity, used by Advaita for empirical matters.
era: from c. 8th c. CE; systematized in Dharmarāja's Vedāntaparibhāṣā

evidence.detail: Advaita manuals list the same six pramāṇas with Bhāṭṭa definitions
the maxim 'in empirical matters, the Bhāṭṭa method' (vyavahāre bhāṭṭanayaḥ) is cited in Advaita (source of the maxim not checked)

what: Rāmānuja's early training under Yādavaprakāśa and the shared pariṇāma and aṃśa readings of the Brahma Sūtras, which Rāmānuja reworked into the body–soul model while criticising both forms of bhedābheda.

evidence.detail: Śrīvaiṣṇava hagiography of Rāmānuja and Yādavaprakāśa
Vedārthasaṅgraha discusses Bhāskara's and Yādava's views

what: The theme of learning from natural teachers: Bodhya's six teachers (Piṅgalā, osprey, snake, bee, arrow-maker, maiden) all reappear among the avadhūta's twenty-four; Piṅgalā's song and maxim recur.
era: between the Mahābhārata's Śāntiparvan and the Bhāgavata (scholarly)

evidence.detail: the tradition treats both as Vyāsa's

what: The figure of Puruṣa Nārāyaṇa and the name of a five-night (pañcarātra) sacrifice

evidence.detail: ŚB 13.6.1.1: Puruṣa Nārāyaṇa beholds the five-night sacrifice and becomes all.
A link to the later Pāñcarātra tradition's name has been proposed; not established.

what: Names of heavens and deva classes in Vyāsa's cosmology (YBh 3.26): Tuṣita, Aparinirmitavaśavartin, Parinirmitavaśavartin, Brahmapurohita, Brahmakāyika, Ābhāsvara, Śuddhanivāsa, and the Avīci hell.

evidence.detail: Same or near-identical names in Buddhist cosmology (Tusita, Paranimmitavasavattī, Brahmapurohita, Ābhassara, Suddhāvāsa, Avīci); Vyāsa also links his highest gods to the meditations with reasoning, reflection, bliss and I-am-ness, as Buddhism links heavens to jhānas.

what: The five means of YS 1.20 — śraddhā, vīrya, smṛti, samādhi, prajñā.

evidence.detail: Identical to the Buddhist five faculties/powers (indriya/bala: saddhā, viriya, sati, samādhi, paññā).
Widely taken as a borrowing from Buddhism.

what: The four attitudes maitrī, karuṇā, muditā, upekṣā (YS 1.33), called 'the abodes (vihāra) of meditators' in YBh 4.10.
era: early centuries CE (YS/YBh) — older Buddhist attestation

evidence.detail: Same four terms as the Buddhist brahmavihāras (Pali mettā, karuṇā, muditā, upekkhā); YBh 4.10 uses 'vihāra'.

Many scholars see Buddhist precedence; others posit a shared śramaṇa milieu (the Jain four bhāvanās maitrī, pramoda, kāruṇya, mādhyasthya — Tattvārtha Sūtra 7 — are also parallel). Direction not settled.

what: Ignorance as taking the impermanent, impure, painful and non-self as permanent, pure, pleasant and self (YS 2.5).

evidence.detail: Parallels the four perversions (vipallāsa) of Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.49 (Vipallāsa Sutta).
Commonly cited as evidence of Buddhist influence on the Yoga Sūtra.

what: The fourfold scheme of the śāstra modelled on medicine — saṃsāra, its cause, liberation, the means (YBh 2.15; YS 2.16–26).

evidence.detail: Compared with the four noble truths and their medical framing in Buddhist texts; the medical model may be common Indian property.

what: The vocabulary of kleśa and anuśaya ('sukhānuśayī rāgaḥ', 'duḥkhānuśayī dveṣaḥ' 2.7–8; 'anuśerate' YBh 2.4), the burnt-seed image, and afflictions as the root of karma.

evidence.detail: kleśa / kilesa; anuśaya is a technical term of Buddhist Abhidharma.
Influence of Sarvāstivāda/Sautrāntika Abhidharma on the Yoga theory of afflictions has been proposed.

what: Meditative vocabulary: samāpatti, vitarka and vicāra, ekāgratā, nirodha, bhāvanā, and YBh 1.20's 'smṛtyupasthāne'.

evidence.detail: samāpatti, vitakka/vicāra (first-jhāna factors), ekaggatā, satipaṭṭhāna.
Vijñānabhikṣu (YV 1.17) cites a Mokṣadharma verse naming vitarka, vicāra and viveka in the first yoga/dhyāna, showing the same vocabulary in the epic.
Structural correspondence of the samāpattis to the jhānas is contested.

what: Verses and similes quoted in the Yoga-bhāṣya with Buddhist parallels.

evidence.detail: YBh 1.47 'prajñāprasādam āruhya ...' ~ Dhammapada 28 ('paññāpāsādam āruyha ...').
YBh 2.42 'yac ca kāmasukhaṃ loke ...' ~ Udāna 2.2 ('yañca kāmasukhaṃ loke ...'); the verse also occurs in the Mahābhārata.
YBh 2.15: the wise one is like an eyeball hurt by a wool thread — a simile also found in the Abhidharmakośabhāṣya (on 6.3) (recalled; check).
YBh 4.33 classifies questions as answerable one-sidedly, by distinction (vibhajya) or not (avacanīya), as Buddhist texts classify ways of answering questions (Aṅguttara 4.42).

what: The critique of birth-caste under the title 'Vajrasūcī' ('diamond needle'): a Buddhist Vajrasūcī (attributed to Aśvaghoṣa; in Chinese to Dharmakīrti) and the Vajrasūci Upaniṣad share title and line of argument.

evidence.detail: same title; both question birth, body and learning as marks of the brāhmaṇa
often read as a Vedāntic reworking of the Buddhist text; the tradition holds the Upaniṣad to be śruti

notes: Buddhist lineage placement is uncertain (Aśvaghoṣa or Dharmakīrti); recorded under lin:early-buddhism pending the Buddhist units.

what: The penance for killing a brahmin - living with the skull of the slain, begging and proclaiming one's deed - as model of the Kāpālika great vow, mediated by the myth of Bhairava.

evidence.detail: The Kūrma Purāṇa tells of the Lord's skull-bearing penance for brahmin-murder and its release at the tīrtha.
Lorenzen and others derive the mahāvrata from the Dharmaśāstra brahmahatyā penance (Manu and Yājñavalkya; verse numbers not checked here).

what: Life-cycle sacraments, including an initiation with sacred thread, recast for Jain householders

evidence.detail: Jinasena's Ādipurāṇa gives Jain versions of the sacraments (kriyās) for householders.

what: Mutual shaping of late scholastic Vedānta: the Advaitasiddhi is organized as a point-by-point reply to the Nyāyāmṛta, and later Mādhva and Advaita commentaries answer each other in turn.

evidence.detail: The Advaitasiddhi follows the order of the Nyāyāmṛta's topics.

what: The Gauḍīya tradition's claim that Caitanya's line descends from Madhva's sampradāya (through Mādhavendra Purī and Īśvara Purī), and its adoption of a list of Madhva's doctrinal points.

evidence.detail: Gauḍīya paramparā lists (Kavi Karṇapūra's Gauragaṇoddeśadīpikā; Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa, 18th c.) place Caitanya in Madhva's line.
The Caitanya-caritāmṛta (Madhya-līlā 9) narrates Caitanya's meeting with Tattvavādī (Mādhva) teachers at Uḍupi and his disagreement with them.
Many scholars and Mādhva writers doubt a real lineage connection; the Gauḍīya doctrine of inconceivable difference-in-identity differs from Dvaita.

notes: Recorded as disputed; details of the paramparā lists and CC chapter reference recalled at low confidence.

what: Dvaita doctrine — Hari's supremacy, Vāyu's primacy, the gradation of souls and deities — set in Kannada song by the Haridāsas, several of them disciples of Mādhva ascetics (Śrīpādarāja, Vyāsatīrtha, Vādirāja); later systematized in Jagannātha Dāsa's Harikathāmṛtasāra.

evidence.detail: Vyāsatīrtha is remembered as the teacher of Purandara Dāsa and Kanaka Dāsa; Śrīpādarāja as the 'grandfather' of the Haridāsas.
Harikathāmṛtasāra expounds tāratamya and Hari-sarvottamatva in Kannada.

notes: U56 owns the Haridāsa lineage; this records only the transmission.

what: Keśava Kāśmīrin's Kramadīpikā (Kṛṣṇa-mantra liturgy) drawn upon in Gauḍīya ritual; shared Braj Rādhā–Kṛṣṇa devotional milieu.

evidence.detail: Haribhaktivilāsa's use of the Kramadīpikā (to verify)

what: the vocabulary of the first meditation (vitarka, vicāra, viveka) and of nirvāṇa

evidence.detail: MBh 12.188.15 names vicāra, vitarka and viveka as arising in 'the first dhyāna', close to the Pali first jhāna formula; the Gītā speaks of brahmanirvāṇa and 'the peace that culminates in nirvāṇa' (6.15)
some scholars see Buddhist influence on the epic here, others common ascetic vocabulary; the direction is disputed and each tradition defines its own terms

what: shared didactic narratives: the father–son dialogue on renunciation and the parable of the man in the well

evidence.detail: MBh 12.169 (the son urging his father to renounce) parallels Uttarādhyayana 14; the parable of the man hanging over a well (MBh 11.5–6) recurs in Jain story literature

what: Early enumerations of principles and the teachers Kapila, Āsuri, Pañcaśikha (Mokṣadharma); the Yuktidīpikā names Janaka, Vasiṣṭha and Dvaipāyana among those who taught the categories.

evidence.detail: Yuktidīpikā on SK 72
whether epic Sāṃkhya is pre-classical or a parallel development is debated

what: enumeration of principles and the discrimination of puruṣa from prakṛti

evidence.detail: the Mokṣadharma names Kapila, Āsuri and Pañcaśikha, the same founders the classical tradition names
epic Sāṃkhya (with its 24/25/26 counts and a Lord) is often held to precede Īśvarakṛṣṇa's non-theistic system; the tradition instead sees the epic as reporting an already existing Sāṃkhya

what: The yoga of the Mokṣadharma and the Gītā; Hiraṇyagarbha as teacher of yoga.

evidence.detail: The Mahābhārata names Hiraṇyagarbha as the knower of yoga (Nārāyaṇīya, recalled); the Yoga commentators make him the first teacher.
Vijñānabhikṣu cites a Mokṣadharma verse on the first yoga (YV 1.17) and the Gītā (Nārāyaṇatīrtha, YSC intro.).

what: yoga vocabulary: practice and dispassion, concentration (dhāraṇā), yoga-power, the faults of yoga, the first meditation with vitarka and vicāra
era: scholarly: epic and early classical period

evidence.detail: BhG 6.35 (abhyāsa and vairāgya) ~ YS 1.12; MBh 12.188.15 (vicāra, vitarka) ~ YS 1.17; MBh 12.289 (dhāraṇā, yogabala)
direction and dating debated

what: The Sāvitrī (Gāyatrī), with Oṃ and the vyāhṛtis, as the mantra of initiation and of the twilight worship

evidence.detail: Gṛhya and dharma texts prescribe imparting the Sāvitrī at upanayana and its daily repetition (Manusmṛti ch. 2, verse numbers not recalled).

what: the Bhagavad Gītā as one of the three canonical sources (prasthānatraya)

evidence.detail: every Vedānta school comments on the Gītā (Śaṅkara, Rāmānuja, Madhva, Nimbārka school, Vallabha school, Gauḍīya)

what: Yogic anatomy — the bulb (kanda), prāṇa and apāna, six centres, the thousand-petalled lotus and the moon at the crown — integrated into Śivayoga

evidence.detail: Direction of influence between Vīraśaiva Śivayoga and haṭha/tantric yoga is not settled.

what: Haṭha doctrine and verses — mudrās, bandhas, khecarī, kumbhakas, the four yogas and four stages — in the expanded southern recensions of the Yoga Upaniṣads.

evidence.detail: Śāṇḍilya 1.23 ≈ Haṭhayogapradīpikā 2.15 (taming breath like lion, elephant, tiger)
Yogakuṇḍalī 2 draws on the Khecarīvidyā; Dhyānabindu and Yogacūḍāmaṇi share verses with the Gorakṣaśataka; the Yogatattva's four yogas and four stages parallel the Dattātreyayogaśāstra
Bouy (1994): the southern Yoga Upaniṣads were expanded from haṭha works, perhaps in the 18th c.; the tradition regards the Upaniṣads as śruti and prior

notes: Texts involved: src:hatha-yoga-pradipika, src:khecarividya, src:goraksasataka, src:dattatreyayogasastra.

what: Ṛṣabha, the first Tīrthaṅkara of the Jains, appears in the Bhāgavata as an avatāra and avadhūta; the Bhāgavata adds a polemical account of the 'Arhat' king
Śaiva ascetic institutions, maṭhas and sites in Karnataka that passed from Kālāmukha to Vīraśaiva hands

evidence.detail: Proposed in modern scholarship (e.g., D. N. Lorenzen's study of the Kāpālikas and Kālāmukhas) that the Kālāmukhas were absorbed into the Vīraśaiva movement; labeled scholarly metadata.
Neither Vīraśaiva account of origins mentions the Kālāmukhas; Allama's birthplace Baḷḷigāve was a known Kālāmukha centre (inscriptions; moderate confidence).

D. N. Lorenzen (1972) and others: several former Kālāmukha centres (including Śrīśaila) later appear as Vīraśaiva seats, and the Kālāmukhas vanish from records as the Vīraśaivas rise; some ascetics may have joined the new movement.

The Vīraśaiva tradition does not derive itself from the Kālāmukhas: the Pañcācārya account has five ācāryas (Reṇuka and others) emerge from liṅgas in each age and teach from the Śaiva Āgamas (Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi); the Liṅgāyata account centres on Basava and the śaraṇas at Kalyāṇa.
Caution: continuity of buildings is not continuity of doctrine; the vacana movement rejected the temple ritual that Kālāmukha priests served.

notes: Recorded as a borrowing, not a dispute, because no tradition text debates it; see dsp:virasaiva-origins.
alt_notes: Both accounts recorded; not reconciled. Specific inscriptional evidence for each transferred site was not checked in this run.

what: The sixteen names of the Kalisantaraṇa, recited in Gauḍīya practice as the mahāmantra (usually with the 'hare kṛṣṇa' half first).

evidence.detail: Gauḍīya teachers regard the Kalisantaraṇa as the śruti source of the mahāmantra

what: Skull-bowl, skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga), six bone ornaments, cremation-ground setting and the figure of the skull-bearing ascetic in the Buddhist Yoginī tantras.

evidence.detail: Yāmuna's six Kāpāla insignia (ear-ornament/necklace, rucaka, earrings, crest-jewel, ash, sacred thread) resemble the six 'seals' worn by Heruka and yogins in the Yoginī tantras (e.g. Hevajra).
Buddhist myth: Heruka subdues Maheśvara/Bhairava and his retinue and takes over their attire and sacred sites (Cakrasaṃvara cycle).
A. Sanderson argues the Yoginī tantras drew on Śaiva Vidyāpīṭha scriptures of Kāpālika character rather than directly on the Atimārga.

what: Non-dual Śaiva formulations of Śakti in the Lakṣmī Tantra

evidence.detail: argued in scholarship that the Lakṣmī Tantra adapts passages from Kashmirian Śaiva works; not verified here

what: The prakāśa-vimarśa metaphysics and Spanda/Pratyabhijñā exegesis used in Śrīvidyā commentary (Jayaratha's Vāmakeśvarīmatavivaraṇa; Maheśvarānanda; the Kāmakalāvilāsa).

evidence.detail: shared doctrinal vocabulary

what: The Kaula ritual and doctrinal frame: kula conduct, the secret use of the five 'M's, the eight bonds (pāśa), the four seats (Kāmarūpa, Pūrṇagiri, Jālandhara, Oḍḍiyāna), yoginī hierarchies and the āmnāya scheme.

evidence.detail: Amṛtānanda's Dīpikā invokes kaulācāra when commenting on YH 2.81; YH 1.41-42 names the four pīṭhas; PKS 1.12 prescribes the five 'M's in secret.
Śrīvidyā is widely held to have emerged within the Kaula 'southern transmission' (dakṣiṇāmnāya) before its South Indian Vedicizing.

what: The Kaula ritual and doctrine (kula/akula, the Kula worship, the Kaula lineages) integrated by Abhinavagupta, taught him by Śambhunātha of Jālandhara.

evidence.detail: Tantrāloka 29; TĀ 5.52 credits Śambhu[nātha]

what: The long-haired, wind-girdled, silent muni of RV 10.136

evidence.detail: Some scholars see in the Keśin and munis a current of ecstatic asceticism distinct from the sacrificial priesthood, later related to the śramaṇa and yogic traditions; the direction and even the existence of the borrowing are disputed. Metadata only.

what: The Krama's twelve Kālīs and Kālasaṅkarṣiṇī, integrated as a form of the śākta means and as the fourth goddess above the Trika triad.

evidence.detail: Tantrāloka 4.148-173; Abhinavagupta's Kramastotra

what: A guru-succession traced through Madhva, and Baladeva's use of Madhva's category of viśeṣa and nine-tenet format.

evidence.detail: Gauragaṇoddeśadīpikā; Prameyaratnāvalī
the affiliation is asserted in later texts, not in the Gosvāmīs' main works

what: Sāṃkhya-yoga dialogues and Kṛṣṇa narrative shared with the epic and its Harivaṃśa

evidence.detail: Brahma Purāṇa 243-245 parallels the Vasiṣṭha-Karāla Janaka dialogue of MBh 12; VP book 5 parallels the Harivaṃśa

what: The term dharmamegha (YS 4.29), also the name of the tenth bodhisattva ground (dharmameghā bhūmi).

evidence.detail: Daśabhūmika Sūtra's tenth bhūmi; YS 4.29 'dharmameghaḥ samādhiḥ'.
Direction and meaning of the shared term debated; in Yoga it precedes kaivalya, in the Mahāyāna it is the culmination of the bodhisattva path.

what: The compound 'prapañcopaśama' with 'śiva' describes the fourth in MāU 7 and the teaching of dependent origination in the dedicatory verse of Nāgārjuna's Mūlamadhyamakakārikā.

evidence.detail: MāU 7, 12 'prapañcopaśamaṃ śivam'; MMK dedication 'prapañcopaśamaṃ śivam'
direction of borrowing, if any, is debated; not asserted here

what: Śaiva Siddhānta ritual procedures (initiation, worship, installation)

evidence.detail: the Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati's Siddhāntasāra is an authority for Kerala tantris

what: Recensions of Siddhānta scriptures adapted to Vīraśaiva use (Candrajñāna, Makuṭa, Vīra)

evidence.detail: Vīraśaiva recensions catalogued by Muktabodha (M00201, M00202, M00608)
